title: Species composition followed less of its spatial warming benchmark than the thermal mean at 49 Finnish moth sites
abstract: We tested whether fast change in a thermal mean also means fast change towards the species composition found at warmer sites. We used Finnish moth species records, European thermal scores and GHCN-CAMS temperature in 1993-2022. Spatial composition directions were trained on early observations outside each focal 100 km block. At 49 sites, presence-based composition followed 45% of its held-out spatial warming benchmark, versus 87% for the matched thermal mean. The paired difference was -42 percentage points, with a conditional 95% jackknife interval from -72 to -13 points. Count weights gave 46% versus 90%. A stricter survey rule and linear-proportion sensitivity retained the smaller composition response. Only 2.8% of squared presence displacement lay along the trained direction. Full spatial transfer gave no clear composition prediction gain over unchanged composition. This constrains the interpretation of the Finnish contrast case: a near-spatial thermal mean need not imply a near-spatial species-composition response. It does not identify a causal warming effect or an ecological mechanism. Habitat gradients, detection, selected sites, nonlinear response and common year shocks remain limits. Source records overlap earlier Finnish studies. Code, aggregate evidence, source hashes and external-data reproduction instructions are supplied.

display.caption: Matched thermal-mean and species-composition ratios at 49 Finnish moth sites. Bars are conditional 95% spatial-block jackknife intervals. Right: squared displacement along the held-out spatial direction. Neither panel estimates a causal climate fraction.
